bivy.name: North Fork Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT junction
bivy.capacity: Small designated hiker camp with a handful of numbered sites; the site is reserved by name on the permit
bivy.water: Reliable year round — Bridge Creek and the North Fork run beside the camp
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round; reserve the specific camp on Recreation.gov or take a walk-up from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee applies.
bivy.notes: This sits right at the junction where the PCT leaves Bridge Creek for the North Fork, roughly ten miles in from the SR 20 trailhead, so it is the natural first-night stop for a party that started late. It is a long way below the climb, which means a very big second day to reach the glacier bivies. Its value is logistical rather than tactical — it shortens the drive-day push without needing a cross-country zone permit. Being a valley-bottom camp in forest, expect bugs through midsummer.

bivy.name: Walker Park Camp
bivy.capacity: Small designated camp, a couple of parties at most
bivy.water: Reliable — sits on the North Fork of Bridge Creek
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit, booked by camp name; same NPS fee structure as any Bridge Creek camp, and it must be carried for the night you actually sleep there.
bivy.notes: Roughly two miles up the North Fork trail from the junction, this is the first camp that meaningfully shortens the walk to the Goode Glacier drainage. The tread to here is still ordinary maintained trail, so it is an easy target even arriving in the dark. Parties usually treat it as a place to shed weight rather than a base, since the climb is still hours of rough ground above. No elevation is recorded — the valley section stays well under 4,000 ft, but no confident figure was sourced.

bivy.name: Grizzly Creek Camp
bivy.capacity: Larger than the other North Fork camps and open to stock parties, so you may be sharing it
bivy.water: Reliable — Grizzly Creek and the North Fork are both at hand
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit reserved by name through Recreation.gov or issued walk-up at Marblemount; per-person and reservation fees apply.
bivy.notes: About four miles up the North Fork trail, this is the last designated camp before the country turns unpleasant, and the practical decision point for the whole approach. A party arriving late, or facing high water, is usually better off sleeping here than committing to the bushwhack and the crossing in poor light.

bivy.name: Fireweed Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT
bivy.capacity: Designated camp with hiker and stock use
bivy.water: Reliable — Bridge Creek
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit, same Recreation.gov / Marblemount walk-up system and the same per-person and reservation fees.
bivy.notes: A Bridge Creek corridor camp on the PCT well short of the North Fork junction, near the Twisp Pass trail area. It is only useful to a Goode party as an overflow choice when the North Fork camps are booked out, which happens in peak season because so few sites serve this valley. Camping here adds miles to an already long approach day. Treat it as a fallback rather than a plan.

bivy.name: Goode Glacier approach bivy, timbered knoll
bivy.capacity: Informal ground for one or two small tents on a timbered knoll
bivy.water: Meltwater from the Goode Glacier drainage nearby, but flow is seasonal and can be a walk away or thin late in the year
bivy.permit: Inside the Goode CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE, not a designated camp — the permit is issued for the zone, party size is capped at six, no campfires, and camping is only allowed on durable ground such as snow, rock or bare earth.
bivy.notes: Reached by leaving the North Fork trail after Grizzly Creek, fording the creek and grinding up timber and scree beside the drainage off the Goode Glacier, this is the classic first bivy under the buttress. Reports differ on whether it is the better choice: it sits noticeably west of the line of travel, so some parties consider the extra push to higher ground worth doing. Sparse timber gives a little shelter, which matters more here than the small elevation saving. Human waste goes in a cathole or is packed out above treeline, and there is no toilet.

bivy.name: Upper bivy in the rock bands east of the buttress toe
bivy.capacity: Tight — commonly described as just enough flat ground for a party of about four
bivy.water: Running meltwater has been found at or near these sites, but it is snow-fed and not dependable once the drainage dries out later in the season
bivy.permit: Goode cross-country zone permit, six-person maximum, no fires, durable surfaces only; zone camping must also keep clear of designated camps and trails by the park's stated distances.
bivy.notes: Sitting in the rock bands just east of where the Northeast Buttress meets the ground, this puts you at the base with a few hundred feet already banked for summit day, which is the argument for grinding past the lower knoll. The exact elevation is reported inconsistently — figures in the 5,400 to 5,600 ft range all refer to broadly the same shelf system, so navigate to the terrain rather than to a number. It is exposed and rocky, so a poor choice in unsettled weather compared with the timbered ground lower down. Confirm you have water before committing to it late in the summer.

bivy.name: Hannegan Camp, below Hannegan Pass
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself
bivy.water: Side streams and snowmelt near camp, but they are seasonal and can dry or go silty by late summer — treat everything and carry a reserve on a hot September approach
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness) — NO North Cascades National Park permit needed here, since the park boundary is still ahead at the pass. What you need is a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Hannegan trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this Forest Service fee site.
bivy.notes: The obvious staging camp for a party that drives up Ruth Creek late and wants the pass behind them early. Because it sits on the forest side of the divide, the paperwork is entirely different from everything down the far side — parking pass only, no Marblemount errand. Road conditions on FS 32 have been unreliable in recent seasons and access has at times stopped short of the trailhead, so confirm before committing to a long drive. The 2026 Chilliwack Complex closures were written to include trails and camps entering the park from this trailhead, which can leave the camp reachable while the country beyond the pass is not.

bivy.name: Boundary Camp
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet
bivy.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
bivy.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. Fire closures in 2026 affected camps and trails on this side of the pass, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.

bivy.name: Copper Lake Camp, Copper Ridge
bivy.capacity: Designated sites for parties of up to four, with a composting toilet and food-storage lockers
bivy.water: The lake is immediately at hand and reliable all season — a real advantage on this ridge
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, picked up at Marblemount. Food, rubbish and scented items must go in the provided lockers or an approved canister.
bivy.notes: Of the three camps strung along Copper Ridge, this is the one that solves water: the others are drier, and one is normally described as having no water source at all, which forces a long carry from lower down. That makes it the sensible high camp for anyone using the ridge as a high traverse toward the Chilliwack drainage rather than dropping straight into the valley. The ridge is exposed and the sites are small, so a party of more than four has to split across permits. Copper Ridge and the wider Copper Loop were inside the 2026 fire closure footprint, and burned ground stays hazardous for years afterward.

bivy.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
bivy.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet
bivy.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
bivy.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. Old-growth valley bottom means it stays cool and damp, so expect wet gear in the morning. The Chilliwack River Trail was among the 2026 closures and its status should be confirmed before a trip is built around it.

bivy.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
bivy.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
bivy.permit: THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
bivy.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. Sources disagree on how usable the alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is, with the cross-border stretch reported at times as heavy bushwhacking, so the length of the trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.

bivy.capacity: 93 sites in the south loop, 19 of them tent-only; standard car-camping capacity per site
bivy.water: Potable water on site during the operating season; Thunder Creek and Diablo Lake alongside
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed. A Recreation.gov reservation and the standard nightly campground fee apply, and the loop is only open roughly mid-May to early September. This does NOT cover any night spent in the backcountry.
bivy.notes: The Thunder Creek trail leaves directly from the south loop, so most parties sleep here the night before rather than driving in from the west at dawn. It is a low forested car camp on Diablo Lake and carries none of the wilderness rules that apply the moment you walk past the trailhead. Book it separately from your climbing permit; the two systems do not talk to each other. Outside the open season you can still park and start walking, but you cannot camp in the loop.

bivy.name: McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
bivy.capacity: A small handful of numbered tent sites, plus a separate stock camp nearby; party size limits are set per site on the permit
bivy.water: Thunder Creek is immediately at hand and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Designated backcountry camp inside North Cascades National Park, so an NPS wilderness permit is required for every night. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through Recreation.gov and about 40% held for walk-ups issued up to 24 hours ahead at Marblemount. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
bivy.notes: The last camp with any infrastructure — a pit toilet, a cook area and a food-hang setup — sitting at about mile 6.7 on an almost flat forest trail, so it is an easy first night rather than a real approach. Most parties treat it as the staging point, then start the steep work early the next morning. Because it is a designated site rather than open country, you are tied to the exact night and site your permit names. FILLING WATER HERE MATTERS: from the creek crossing upward there is nothing dependable until you are near 6,000 ft.

bivy.name: Tricouni Camp, Thunder Creek trail
bivy.capacity: Small designated hiker camp, a few sites
bivy.water: Fisher Creek and Thunder Creek nearby, reliable through the climbing season
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit system and fees as McAllister — designated site, part reservable and part held for walk-up at Marblemount.
bivy.notes: Despite sharing the peak's name this camp is about a mile and a half further up the valley than the point where climbers leave the trail, so it is a fallback rather than a first choice. It is worth knowing about when McAllister is booked out on the night you need, since a short extra walk each way costs less than losing the trip. The forest here is more open than at McAllister. Nothing about it shortens the climb.

bivy.name: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
bivy.capacity: Rock shelves and slabs above the lake; realistically two or three tents on good ground, and the party limit for the cross-country zone is small
bivy.water: Meltwater and the lake itself, dependable in summer; earlier in the year you may be melting snow
bivy.permit: CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE camping, not a designated site, and the rules differ sharply. The zone covering this basin does not accept advance reservations, so in practice it is WALK-UP ONLY from Marblemount, up to 24 hours before you start. Quotas are tiny — a small number of parties per night, with a low maximum party size — so a weekend plan can simply fail at the counter. Confirm the zone name and its current quota with the WIC rather than assuming.
bivy.notes: The working base camp for both summits, on slabs and rubble near where the lower glacier has withdrawn into a lake. Ground is sloping and loose in places, so finding two flat platforms takes some hunting; camp on rock, snow or bare ground and stay well back from the water. Zone rules mean no fires, and human waste goes out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier. Allow the whole day to get here from the valley — parties routinely underestimate it. The steep climbers' trail above McAllister gains roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles.

bivy.name: Lucky Pass bivy, Primus-Tricouni col
bivy.capacity: One or two parties at most, on rock and snow; nothing prepared
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable late in the season once the col melts out
bivy.permit: Still inside the same cross-country zone as the Borealis camp, so the same walk-up-only permit, small party limit and blue-bag requirement apply. A permit issued for the zone covers a bivy here; it does not entitle you to camp wherever you like across zone boundaries.
bivy.notes: The col between the two peaks is high, exposed and windy, and it exists as an option rather than a plan — a spot to sit out weather or finish a day that ran long. Both summits are short from here, which tempts people, but hauling camp another 1,200 ft is rarely worth it against a comfortable night lower down.
